title: Mengu I'di
author: Ssalongo Ssali
desc: Mangoes cooked, the juice squeezed out while they are cooling, and sugar stirred in — the squeezing has to happen warm.
longDesc: Mengu i'di is cooked mango juice, and the one instruction that matters is the timing: the juice is squeezed out while the fruit is cooling, not hot and not cold. Hot, you cannot handle it; cold, the pulp holds on to the liquid. It is a Lugbara drink and it belongs to the same family as the pineapple-peel omunanansi — a drink made by cooking fruit that is too ripe, too plentiful, or both.
steps: Squeeze the juice out while they are cooling.
chefTips: Squeeze while cooling. That is the whole technique and the source is specific about it — hot fruit burns your hands and cold pulp will not give up its juice.
Very ripe mangoes are what this is for, the same way omunanansi is for over-ripe pineapples. It is a glut drink.
Squeeze by hand through cloth rather than blending, as with the passion fruit in UGA045. Blending shreds fibre into the juice.
Sugar to taste, at the end. No quantity is documented.

It belongs to a set of Lugbara drinks: ebe'de or ibe'de is the unsweetened self-service tea named after the scooping action; kuruku chai is lemongrass boiled in tea, UGA115; anya i'di is millet porridge with groundnut or sesame paste; maize milk is UGA100.
No quantities and no cooking time are documented anywhere. Nothing here is estimated.
Chill it before serving if you can. Warm fruit juice tastes markedly more acidic.
sources: Adapted from the Wikipedia article on Lugbara cuisine, which lists mengu i'di as cooked mango with the juice squeezed while cooling and mixed with sugar. That is the entirety of the documented method and no quantities or timings are given.

The related Lugbara drinks named in that article are carried in the tips: ebe'de or ibe'de, unsweetened tea named after the scooping action and taken self-service; kuruku chai, lemongrass boiled in tea; anya i'di, millet porridge with groundnut or sesame paste; and maize milk.
The hand-squeezing-rather-than-blending practice is drawn from the documented Ugandan passion fruit juice in UGA045 and is a cross-reference rather than an attestation for this drink.
That article carries only three references, including web archives and blog material, so its detail is treated as a lead rather than as established fact.
reheating: Served cold, or warm if you prefer.
healthBenefits: Mangoes are very high in vitamins A and C.
Cooking loses some vitamin C but makes the fruit keep.
Sweetened to taste, so the sugar is under your control.
culturalNote: Cooking fruit to make a drink rather than eating it fresh is a preservation move, and West Nile mangoes come all at once. It is the same logic as omunanansi's boiled pineapple peelings — nothing is wasted and nothing is eaten only one way.
